title: Molecular Epidemiology and Risk Factors of Theileria annulata Infection and Rhipicephalus and Hyalomma Tick Infestation in Three Districts of Northern Pakistan.
abstract: Ticks and tick-borne diseases pose a major threat to livestock productivity in tropical and subtropical regions, by transmitting pathogens of veterinary and public health concern, including Theileria species. Despite the threats posed to the large ruminant industry, integrated studies on the causative agent of tropical theileriosis and its tick vectors from the same infected hosts, along with their associated risk factors, remain limited in northern Pakistan. This study investigated Theileria infection, its associated tick species, and host- and environmental-related risk factors in large ruminants from the region using an integrated approach. A total of 3151 ticks (female: 1630, 51.7%; male: 725, 23%; nymph: 458, 14.5%; larvae: 338, 10.7%) were collected from 900 animals (805 cattle, 89.45%; 95 buffaloes, 10.55%), along with 221 blood samples from symptomatic, tick infested animals (202 cattle, 91.4%; 19 buffaloes, 8.6%) between May 2024 and April 2025. Ticks were identified morphologically, while Theileria infection was assessed by microscopy and PCR targeting the 18S rRNA gene. Phylogenetic analysis was performed in MEGA X using the maximum-likelihood method. Host- and environmental-related risk factors were assessed for their association with tick infestation and Theileria infection. Two tick genera were identified morphologically: Rhipicephalus (83.59%) and Hyalomma (16.41%). Within Rhipicephalus, Rhipicephalus microplus (70.29%) was the dominant species, followed by Rhipicephalus haemaphysaloides (7.61%) and Rhipicephalus sp. (5.68%). The genus Hyalomma comprised Hyalomma anatolicum (8.82%) and Hyalomma turanicum (7.58%). Tick infestation was significantly higher in cattle (46.33%) than in buffaloes (22.11%). In cattle, infestation rates were 46.49% in Upper Dir, 46.62% in Bajaur and 45.90% in Lower Dir, whereas in buffaloes, the corresponding rates were 24.14%, 23.53% and 18.75%, respectively. Microscopic examination detected Theileria infection in 18.09% (40/221) of blood samples from clinically affected, tick-infested animals (37/202 cattle, 18.31%; 3/19 buffaloes, 15.78%), whereas the detection rate by PCR was 45.24% (100/221) (92/202 cattle, 45.54%; 8/19 buffaloes, 42.11%). By BLAST analysis, the obtained sequence of 18S rRNA showed a maximum identity of 99.62% with a Theileria annulata sequence from Turkey, China and Pakistan, and phylogenetic tree grouped it with corresponding species from Asia and Europe. Risk factors analysis showed that host species was significantly associated with tick infestation, while age, season, and acaricide treatment were significantly associated with infestation in both cattle and buffaloes (p < 0.05). Age, season and acaricide use were significantly associated with Theileria infection in cattle, whereas in buffaloes, only acaricide use was significant. Gender, presence of rural poultry, grazing system and district showed no significant association (p > 0.05) with tick infestation or Theileria infection in either host. This study provides an integrated assessment of the causative agent of tropical theileriosis and associated tick species from the same large ruminants, along with their associated risk factors, in the mountainous terrain of northern Pakistan. Given that tick vectors and tropical theileriosis can significantly affect livestock-dependent economies, this study may help guide better preventive measures in the region.

title: Variant escape site mapping and characterization of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid rapid antigen test antibodies.
abstract: Rapid antigen tests (RATs) were a critical tool for diagnosing severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection during the height of the pandemic, but their performance depends on antibodies that remain robust to viral evolution. Since most commercial RATs target the viral nucleocapsid protein, mutations in this domain can compromise binding and test performance. To systematically define this risk, we used deep mutational scanning (DMS) to map escape mutations for 82 antibodies across 43 commercially available tests, generating the most comprehensive escape database of SARS-CoV-2 viral mutations to date. Most antibodies target conformational epitopes, with 47 (57%) mapping to the RNA-binding domain and 23 (28%) to the dimerization domain. Principal component analysis and clustering revealed escape phenotypes, including shared features outside of predicted epitopes. As the pandemic proceeded, we noted a change in industry preference from IgG to IgM-type antibodies, which was associated with changes to epitope sub-class prevalence. Analysis of paired capture-detection antibodies revealed a preference for targeting the same structural domain (20/33 or 61%), indicating a slight preference for test antibodies to hit orthogonal yet proximal sites. Together, the results establish a comprehensive resource for understanding how SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein mutations affect antibody binding and the phenotypes that underlie RAT antibody selection. This resource and approach can help prioritize antibodies for follow-up performance testing and support the design of more mutation-resilient diagnostics.IMPORTANCEIt is critical during a pandemic for diagnostic tests to be accurate and for the false negative rate to be kept low. The rapidly changing nature of SARS-CoV-2 exposed a weakness with using rapid antigen tests to diagnose infection, as mutations to the viral nucleocapsid protein can cause the virus to evade detection. In this work, we systematically tested the robustness of 82 antibodies from 43 separate commercially available tests by deliberately mutating the nucleocapsid protein and investigating which changes caused weakened binding to the test antibodies. In addition to determining which specific tests were at risk from certain mutations, we collated our datasets into a meta-analysis, allowing us to identify some best practices for designing robust tests. We, therefore, expect that this resource will support the design of more mutation-resilient diagnostics, whether for future variants of SARS-CoV-2 or in applying these principles to other respiratory viruses, such as influenza virus.

title: Environmental contamination with canine soil-transmitted helminths in New Zealand urban areas: A nationwide molecular, spatial, and risk factor analysis survey.
abstract: Urban parks and recreational areas are frequent gathering sites for dogs and their owners, where dog waste creates sources for pathogens of veterinary and zoonotic concern. Canine soil-transmitted helminths (cSTHs) such as hookworms (Ancylostoma spp. and Uncinaria stenocephala), roundworms (Toxocara canis and Toxascaris leonina), whipworms (Trichuris vulpis), and threadworms (Strongyloides stercoralis), are recognised for their ability to cause gastrointestinal disease and other health issues in dogs. In addition, some species are known for being zoonotic and cause potentially life-threatening conditions in humans. In an exploratory investigation performed in 2023, canine faecal samples were collected from 16 areas across five regions in New Zealand and screened using antigen-based tests, revealing that overall, 31.3% (95% CI 14.2-55.6) of areas were contaminated with at least one parasite, with 7.1% (95% CI 3.3-14.6) and 3.5% (95% CI 1.2-9.9) of individual samples testing positive for roundworms and whipworms, respectively. In a subsequent nationwide survey in 2024, 739 canine faecal samples were collected from 123 urban areas across New Zealand and analysed using multiplex real-time PCRs. Positive samples were further genetically characterised by Sanger and nanopore sequencing. Overall, 24.4% (95% CI 17.7-32.7) of areas tested positive for at least one cSTH, most commonly Ancylostoma caninum (12.2%, 95% CI 7.5-19.1), followed by Uncinaria stenocephala (9.8%, 95% CI 5.7-16.3), T. canis (3.3%, 95% CI 1.3-8.1), and T. vulpis (1.6%, 95% CI 0.4-5.7), whilst Ancylostoma ceylanicum and S. stercoralis were not detected. Logistic regression analyses identified dog density, proximity to city centres, and bioclimatic zone, as predictors of cSTHs contamination in urban areas. This study provides in depth information on the molecular identity and spatial distribution of cSTHs in New Zealand's urban areas and contributes to understanding environmental exposure risk to support parasite surveillance and control in companion animals.

title: Emergence of OXA-48-producing
abstract: Carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae (CP-KP) represents a major public health threat. The global dissemination of antimicrobial resistance is largely driven by high-risk clones (HRCs), such as ST307/OXA-48, ST11/OXA-48 and ST512/KPC-3, which currently dominate the epidemiology of CP-KP in Spain. This study aimed to describe the emergence, dissemination and genomic evolution of an OXA-48-producing K. pneumoniae ST5994 clone in Cantabria, Spain, and to characterize its genomic, phenotypic and epidemiological features. A retrospective genomic surveillance study of CP-KP isolates was conducted in Cantabria from 2021 to 2024. Whole-genome sequencing was used to characterize sequence types, resistome, mobilome, virulome, pangenome and phylogenetic relationships. Antimicrobial susceptibility and biofilm production assays were performed. Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy combined with machine learning algorithms was used to develop a rapid method for HRCs discrimination. Among 448 non-duplicate CP-KP isolates, bla OXA-48 was the predominant carbapenemase. K. pneumoniae ST5994 was first detected in the second quarter of 2023 and rapidly became one of the dominant CP-KP clones at both reference hospital and regional levels over a two-year period, displacing previously prevalent HRCs, such as K. pneumoniae ST11 and K. pneumoniae ST307. The newly identified clone harbored two potentially conjugative plasmids carrying bla OXA-48 carbapenemase and bla CTX-M-15 extended-spectrum beta-lactamase. At the time of writing, eight ST5994 genomes were publicly available, all from the Americas and none carrying a bla OXA-48 gene, therefore this study represents both the first description of this ST in Europe and its first association with OXA-48. Genomic and epidemiological analyses were compatible with sustained dissemination within the regional healthcare network, although the specific transmission pathways could not be established with the available data. Comparative analyses supported a close evolutionary relationship between K. pneumoniae ST307 and ST5994. Our findings highlight the rapid emergence and regional replacement capacity of the novel OXA-48-producing K. pneumoniae ST5994. The integration of genomic and phenotypic data provides insights into its evolutionary trajectory and transmission dynamics. Furthermore, the proposed FT-IR-based approach combined with machine learning offers a promising tool for rapid discrimination of HRCs, supporting surveillance and infection control strategies.
journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

title: Emergence of the GI-23 lineage of infectious bronchitis virus in Brazilian backyard poultry.
abstract: Infectious bronchitis virus (IBV) remains a major threat to poultry production worldwide, with the GI-23 lineage emerging as one of the most epidemiologically relevant variants in recent years. Although GI-23 has been reported in Brazilian commercial poultry, its occurrence and genomic characteristics in backyard poultry remain poorly understood. This study investigated the molecular epidemiology and evolutionary features of IBV circulating in backyard poultry from São Paulo State, Brazil. Samples from 893 backyard birds were screened for IBV using RT-qPCR targeting the 5' untranslated region (5'UTR). Positive samples were further characterized by lineage-specific RT-PCR assays, S1 gene sequencing, virus isolation, and whole-genome sequencing, followed by phylogenetic, phylogenomic, and recombination analyses. IBV was detected exclusively in chickens, with an overall prevalence of 13.8% (42/304 swab pools; 95% CI: 10.1-18.2). Among RT-qPCR-positive samples, 23.9% were identified as belonging to the GI-23 lineage, while GI-1 and GI-11 lineages were not detected. Phylogenetic analysis of partial S1 gene sequences revealed multiple GI-23 sublineages circulating in Brazil, indicating different viral introductions. Whole-genome sequencing of a Brazilian GI-23 isolate showed high identity to a virus identified in Mexico and revealed recombination events involving European and Middle Eastern IBV lineages. These findings provide the molecular and genomic evidence of IBV GI-23 circulation in Brazilian backyard poultry and highlight the importance of monitoring viral evolution and supporting effective disease control strategies.
authors: Paulo Roberto Blandino de Lima Dias
journal: Avian pathology : journal of the W.V.P.A

title: Heterogeneous co-circulation of multiple DENV-1 and DENV-2 genotypes in Vung Tau during the 2023 dengue outbreak in Vietnam.
abstract: Dengue virus (DENV) remains a significant global health threat, particularly in hyper-endemic regions like Vietnam, where the co-circulation of multiple serotypes and genotypes complicates disease control. In 2023, 6.5 million dengue cases and 6,800 deaths were reported globally, marking the largest dengue outbreak in the world. Vietnam recorded 149,557 dengue cases and 36 deaths, with a notable dominance of the DENV-2 serotype. This study provides a comprehensive genomic characterization of the 2023 outbreak using isolates collected from hospitalized patients (n = 148; 66.89% adults). To ensure robust viral recovery, we propagated 90 isolates using a low-passage, antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE)-based system. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of 53 isolates yielded 47 consensus sequences, including 26 complete genomes. Phylogenetic analysis revealed the simultaneous co-circulation of diverse DENV-1 and DENV-2 genotypes. DENV-1 isolates were predominantly genotype I (86%), clustering closely with prior Vietnamese strains and suggesting sustained endemic maintenance, while genotype IV (14%) was detected sporadically. Among DENV-2 isolates, the Cosmopolitan genotype was predominant (98%), with a smaller proportion (2%) belonging to the Asian 1 genotype. Both genotypes clustered with previously reported Vietnamese and regional Southeast Asian strains, indicating ongoing local circulation and regional viral exchange. Comparative mutational analysis of DENV-2 Cosmopolitan isolates identified multiple non-synonymous amino acid substitutions across the viral genome. Fourteen substitutions were shared between Vietnamese historical (2019-2022) and 2023 isolates, while 24 substitutions were unique to the 2023 outbreak strains. The majority of amino acid changes were concentrated within the NS5, E, NS1, and NS3 proteins, suggesting continued genetic diversification within the circulating Cosmopolitan lineage. Overall, these findings demonstrate the persistence of established DENV lineages alongside ongoing viral evolution during the 2023 outbreak in Vietnam. This study highlights the value of whole-genome surveillance for monitoring dengue virus genetic diversity and provides insight that may support future epidemiological surveillance, vaccine evaluation, and outbreak preparedness.
